I am 62 years old, and I have been farming these 12 mu in Quzhou for 40 years. I never went to school, but I know this land with my hands and my eyes. My husband and I are the only ones left in the household, so we cannot manage too much labor‑intensive crop. That is why I keep 8 mu under the wheat‑maize rotation and 4 mu under cotton. The wheat‑maize system gives us steady grain and income with less hand labor, especially since the village has machines for rotary tillage and no‑tillage sowing. Cotton brings higher prices per mu, but it is back‑breaking work—planting, pruning, topping, and picking all by hand. Still, 4 mu is just enough for the two of us to handle, and we are used to it.

It is now early spring, and my winter wheat is already in the ground. I sowed it last October with an improved variety like Shimai 22. I will irrigate it once at green‑up and top‑dress it with urea. I will irrigate two more times before harvest—at jointing and grain‑filling. After harvest in early June, I will immediately sow hybrid maize using no‑tillage into the wheat stubble. Maize needs less fuss; I will give it basal compound fertilizer at sowing, top‑dress urea at the big trumpet stage, and irrigate twice if the summer rains are not enough. I will spray herbicide once for weeds and insecticide once if I see armyworms. After maize harvest in late September, I will rotary till the soil and sow winter wheat again in mid‑October.

For the 4 mu of cotton, I will rotary till in late April and sow an improved Bt cotton variety like Guoxinmian. I will apply compound fertilizer as basal and urea at flowering. Cotton needs water at seedling, flowering, and boll stages, so I will irrigate three times from my well. I know cotton pests are troublesome, so I will spray pesticide about eight times through the season to control bollworm, aphids, and mites. I expect to start picking in September and continue into October.

I keep my fertilizer use moderate—about 20 kg of nitrogen per mu for wheat, 18 kg for maize, and 15 kg for cotton. Fertilizer is expensive now, and I have learned that putting on too much does not always mean more yield. My well gives reliable water, but pumping costs electricity, so I do not waste water.
